findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Financing costs consumed a higher proportion of revenue than budgeted
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream came in at 19.07% against an estimate of 17.69%, a 1.38 percentage point increase. This means debt service is taking a larger share of the council's available revenue than expected.
findings.matters: A rising financing cost ratio reduces the council's flexibility to respond to other pressures and increases the structural cost of its existing debt. For a lender, this indicates less headroom for managing revenue volatility.
findings.figures: Actual 19.07%, estimate 17.69%, variance 1.38%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Working balances came in materially below the mid-year revised forecast
findings.detail: Actual core funds of £39.209m fell significantly short of the revised estimate of £52.138m, a shortfall of £12.929m (25% below revised). This indicates the council's cash position tightened unexpectedly during the year and suggests either unplanned spending or lower-than-expected income.
findings.matters: Working balances are the buffer against unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. A £12.9m variance on a revised estimate signals the council could not maintain expected liquidity, which matters to lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Core Funds / Working Balances actual £39,209k, revised estimate £52,138k, variance (£12,929k)
findings.quote: Core Funds / Working Balances (42,387) (52,138) (39,209) 12,929

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Major local government reorganisation scheduled for 2028 — councils transitioning from two-tier to new structure
findings.detail: The Government plans to reconfigure local authority structures, moving away from the two-tier system. Lancashire, where Chorley sits, is included in this reorganisation. The council is actively engaged in programme arrangements to support transition to new organisations from 2028, with a March 2027 deadline for maintaining robust governance during this transition.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisation creates uncertainty and diverts senior management capacity away from current operations. It presents a material governance risk period with potential for control gaps as responsibilities shift between organisations.
findings.figures: Transition to complete by 2028
findings.quote: The Government has set out plans to move away from the current two-tier system of district and county councils and this includes Lancashire.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Data Protection compliance audit undertaken by external specialist — indicating previous gaps
findings.detail: An external specialist company has been commissioned to audit GDPR and Data Protection compliance. The audit is expected to identify gaps and issue recommendations. This item was carried forward from the previous year's improvement actions, indicating compliance concerns were not fully resolved.
findings.matters: GDPR compliance failures can result in regulatory penalties and reputational damage. The need for external specialist audit suggests internal capability or compliance gaps.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: An audit is being undertaken by an external company who are specialist in Data Protection. The audit will identify any gaps and issue recommendations if required.

findings.detail: The 2024/25 external audit (concluded November 2025) continued to make 5 recommendations for improvements. The 11 recommendations from the prior year audit were either completed or mitigated to the extent currently possible, but the persistence of new issues indicates ongoing audit concerns.
findings.matters: Continuing external audit recommendations indicate that previously identified issues are not fully resolved and new control issues are emerging.
findings.figures: 5 recommendations in 2024/25 audit; 11 carried forward from prior year
findings.quote: The most recent review undertaken (which is for the period 2024/25 concluded in November 2025) whilst continuing to make 5 recommendations for improvements

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal audit identifies control design weaknesses and inconsistent application of governance controls
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit concluded that governance arrangements were generally adequate, but explicitly identified control design weaknesses and inconsistent application, particularly in cross-cutting governance reviews. The audit states these matters increase the risk to achieving specific objectives and require management attention.
findings.matters: Control design weaknesses directly increase financial and operational risk. Inconsistent application across the council suggests governance controls cannot be reliably depended upon.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: However, some control design weaknesses and instances of inconsistent application have been identified, particularly in relation to cross-cutting governance reviews. These matters increase the risk to the achievement of specific objectives and require management attention.

findings.headline: Deputy Chief Executive departed — replacement recruitment unsuccessful
findings.detail: The Deputy Chief Executive left in January 2026. Following an unsuccessful recruitment exercise, the council is considering further options. However, the wider Senior Leadership Team has remained largely stable.
findings.matters: A vacant Deputy Chief Executive role represents a leadership gap at the most senior level, with potential implications for strategic decision-making and control oversight.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Deputy Chief Executive departed in January 2026 and, following an unsuccessful recruitment exercise, further options are currently being considered.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Monitoring Officer role vacant — interim arrangements in place while permanent recruitment continues
findings.detail: The Director of Governance left the council in early 2025, and the statutory Monitoring Officer role has been fulfilled by interim arrangements pending a permanent appointment. A Deputy Monitoring Officer has provided support throughout, but the senior governance lead remains unfilled.
findings.matters: The Monitoring Officer is the statutory officer responsible for ensuring lawful decision-making and compliance with regulations. A prolonged vacancy means this critical control function is not permanently established, which increases governance risk.
findings.figures: None provided

findings.paper_title: Appendix B2: Risks to the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Council's major income streams (planning, garden waste, car parking, commercial assets) face external risk outside council control
findings.detail: The council's significant income sources include planning fees, garden waste subscriptions, car parking, and commercial income from assets it owns. The document notes reductions in income outside the council's control could leave services under-funded, and the council has prudently set aside an income equalisation reserve.
findings.matters: These are discretionary income sources vulnerable to external shocks; their volatility affects financial stability and sustainability of services
findings.figures: Minimum general fund balance set at £4m
findings.quote: The major income streams that the council benefits from include planning, garden waste subscriptions and car parking, as well as commercial income from assets the council owns. Reductions in income outside the control of the council could leave services under-funded.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B2: Risks to the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation scheduled for 1 April 2028 is not provided for anywhere in the MTFS
findings.detail: The current timetable for Lancashire reorganisation would create new unitary authorities from 1 April 2028. This occurs during the MTFS period but the document states explicitly that the strategy makes no provision for impact or changes this would lead to. The council acknowledges fundamental changes cannot be foreseen.
findings.matters: Structural change midway through the strategy period creates material planning uncertainty; the absence of any provision suggests the impact on finances and borrowing has not been modelled
findings.figures: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The current timetable for reorganisation across Lancashire would lead to new unitaries formed from 1 April 2028. The MTFS makes no provision for the impact or changes this would lead to but clearly this would be within the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B2: Risks to the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Council faces forecast budget deficits of £0.845m in 2027/28 and £1.738m in 2028/29 with no detailed savings plan yet identified
findings.detail: The MTFS includes specific forecast cumulative deficits that will require further development of a savings programme and income generation to close them. Monitoring is overseen by Senior Management and Leadership teams. The council has significant dependency on commercial income which carries risks outside its control.
findings.matters: Deficits of this scale demonstrate material budget pressure; the fact the council still needs to 'further develop' the savings programme indicates solutions are not yet confirmed
findings.quote: The MTFS includes forecast cumulative gross budget deficits of £0.845m and £1.738m in 2027/28 and 2028/29 respectively. To balance the budget over the course of the MTFS we will need to further develop the savings programme, including opportunities for income generation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B2: Risks to the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Business rates account for 40% of council income and face system change uncertainty during the MTFS period
findings.detail: The government is undertaking significant changes to the business rates system including new multipliers, rebasing and re-measurement. Business Rate Pooling has been made effectively redundant in 2026/27. The council must make difficult annual assumptions on write-offs, appeals, growth and reliefs, with complexity increased by higher multipliers.
findings.matters: Business rates is material to revenue funding; uncertainty around system changes creates in-year income volatility risk and could affect borrowing capacity and financial stability
findings.figures: 40% of council's income
findings.quote: As Business Rates account for approximately 40% of the council's income, this is a significant risk; Whilst the government allowed for Business Rate Pooling to continue the impact of the reforms to business rates effectively made pooling redundant in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D: Cumulative Budget Deficit & Budget Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Budget delivery depends on £1,000k+ in 'Fit for the Future' savings proposals of uncertain realization
findings.detail: The budget assumes delivery of major savings initiatives across multiple services: car parking strategy (£200k), planning income (£100k), leisure services (£100k), bus station review (£150k), town centre regeneration (£100k), and others. Many require service changes or new income streams. Failure to deliver these proposals would widen the existing budget deficit.
findings.matters: Budgets that rely on discretionary savings rather than automatic funding carry higher execution risk. If Fit for the Future proposals do not materialize, the council faces an additional budget crisis on top of the already-identified £1.7m deficit.
findings.figures: Fit for the Future proposals total £1,000k+: Car Parking (£200k), Planning (£100k), Council Assets (£70k), Customer Services (£75k), Leisure (£100k), Bus Station (£150k), Town Centre (£100k)
findings.quote: Fit for the Future Proposals: Develop and deliver a Car Parking Strategy (200); Review Planning Service Income generation (100); Deliver the Leisure Services Development Action Plan (100); Review of the Bus Station Operating Model (150)

findings.paper_title: Appendix D: Cumulative Budget Deficit & Budget Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant falls by £1,104k over three years, from £4,656k to £3,552k
findings.detail: Central government funding declines structurally: Fair Funding Assessment Revenue Support Grant reduces from £4,656k in 2026/27 to £3,552k by 2028/29. This £1,104k reduction is outside the council's control and directly worsens the budget position by removing available funding.
findings.matters: Falling government grants force all budget adjustments to come from discretionary savings or service reductions. Structural revenue loss combined with rising costs indicates sustained financial pressure the council cannot escape.
findings.quote: Fair Funding Assessment - Revenue Support Grant (4,656) (4,119) (3,552)

findings.paper_title: Appendix D: Cumulative Budget Deficit & Budget Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: FCC waste contract uplift of £1,129k in 2026/27 plus £491k Extended Producer Responsibility adds major fixed costs
findings.detail: The FCC contract (waste and environmental services) adds £1,129k cost in 2026/27, with ongoing inflation pressures of £150k in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Waste Extended Producer Responsibility adds a further £491k. Together these amount to £1,620k of fixed, externally-driven costs in the first year alone.
findings.matters: Waste contracts are long-term, largely fixed commitments that consume budget flexibility. These costs demonstrate how externally-driven pressures (inflation, regulatory requirements) can overwhelm a council's ability to manage its finances.
findings.figures: FCC Contract uplift £1,129k (2026/27); FCC inflation £150k (2027/28 and 2028/29); Waste Extended Producer Responsibility £491k (2026/27)
findings.quote: FCC Contract uplift 1,129; Waste Extended Producer Responsibility (491)

findings.paper_title: Appendix D: Cumulative Budget Deficit & Budget Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Budget deficit grows to £1,738k by 2028/29 as expenditure exceeds financing
findings.detail: Total expenditure reaches £18,555k in 2028/29 but total financing is only £16,817k, creating a structural deficit of £1,738k. A £845k gap also appears in 2027/28. This shortfall cannot be covered by normal operations and will require reserve drawdown, additional savings, or increased borrowing.
findings.matters: A growing budget deficit of this magnitude signals financial deterioration and indicates the council will need to either find additional savings or increase borrowing to balance its budget—material risks for lenders.
findings.quote: Net Expenditure / Budget Gap - 845 1,738

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: One-off £650k pension saving from revaluation unlikely to recur; masks underlying deficit
findings.detail: A triannual revaluation of the Lancashire Pension Fund in Autumn 2025 produced exceptional surpluses, cutting employer contribution rates from 18.3% to 9.8%. This generates approximately £650k in savings for 2026/27 but is non-recurring. The next revaluation (2028) is likely to reverse these gains.
findings.matters: The 2026/27 balanced budget depends heavily on this one-off windfall. When it disappears, the council will need to find an additional £650k in savings or face a combined deficit of ~£500k in 2027/28—larger than currently forecast.
findings.figures: £650k saving, contribution rate change from 18.3% to 9.8%
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of the consultation the reduction for Chorley Council is from 18.3% to 9.8% (8.5%)

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: £60m capital programme planned while revenue budget deteriorates to £1.738m deficit
findings.detail: The council is planning £60m of capital investment over three years, including major projects: town centre transformation (£44m), leisure centre improvements (£4.5m), and residential development (£6.6m). This ambitious capital programme must be financed and repaid alongside revenue spending that moves into significant deficits.
findings.matters: Large capital investment while revenue position worsens will increase borrowing and debt service costs, compounding financial stress. If conditions deteriorate, projects may need deferral, creating reputational and financial complications.
findings.figures: £60m total capital 2026–2029; £44m town centre, £4.5m leisure, £6.6m residential
findings.quote: The capital programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 totals £60.000m and is an indication of how ambitious the council is in delivering its Corporate Strategy

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Council froze council tax in 2026/27 despite settlement allowing up to 3% increase
findings.detail: The government's finance settlement allows district councils to raise council tax by up to 3% per band D property. Chorley chose to freeze the rate, citing the difficult financial climate for residents. This decision reduces discretionary income by approximately £250–300k that could otherwise have been raised.
findings.matters: While defensible as policy, freezing council tax during mounting deficits limits revenue flexibility and increases reliance on central government funding (which is being cut) or borrowing.
findings.figures: Settlement permitted up to 3% increase; freeze represents foregone income of ~£250–300k
findings.quote: Following consultation and recognising the difficult financial climate for our residents there is a proposed freeze in Council Tax 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 reduces government grant funding by £400k from 2027/28 despite transitional protection
findings.detail: The government's new funding formula initially proposed a significantly lower baseline for Chorley. Transitional protection was introduced but only protects funding to 2025/26 levels. From 2027/28 onwards, the council loses £400k annually in government support—a structural, permanent reduction outside the council's control.
findings.matters: Structural reductions in government funding are irreversible and compound the council's deficit problem. This cut occurs precisely when deficits begin to emerge, narrowing the council's options.
findings.figures: £400k annual reduction from 2027/28
findings.quote: While transitional protection is incorporated into the figures it still means a reduction from 2027/28 of £400k as protection is only afforded to 2025/26 funding levels.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Savings programme incomplete beyond 2027/28; unidentified savings needed to close £1.738m 2028/29 deficit
findings.detail: The Fit for the Future programme identified £1.602m of potential savings but delivery is bunched: £1.2m in 2026/27, £390k in 2027/28, with no named savings for 2028/29 despite a £1.738m deficit. The council states that work has begun on further options but these are not yet identified or approved.
findings.matters: A savings plan with unidentified future elements creates execution risk. If the programme stalls or yields less than forecast, the council will lack a credible way to close the deficit.
findings.figures: £1.602m identified (timing split: £1.2m, £390k); £1.738m 2028/29 deficit requiring further unidentified savings
findings.quote: The programme is on track to save approximately £1.2m in 2026/27 with most elements either already in place or forecast to be in place by 1 April 2026. There is a further £390k identified for 2027/28 and work has begun on further options to be brought forward to address budget gaps.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: New food waste collection requirement adds £1.129m annual pressure with no government funding identified
findings.detail: The council is required to implement weekly food waste collections under central government directive but the government has not provided funding. The council had assumed this would be covered by New Burdens funding but this has not been allocated, creating an unfunded statutory obligation that must be absorbed.
findings.matters: A structural cost increase imposed by law with no funding forces the council to find offsetting cuts, increase borrowing, or cut other services. This reduces the reliability of future budgets.
findings.quote: There appeared to be no new funding in respect of food waste revenue costs which the Council had assumed would be funded by New Burdens funding due to this being a new statutory requirement placed on the council. As such a potential further pressure of £1.129m would be incorporated within the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026/27 Medium Term Financial Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-2029 Accessiblereporttemplate CBC
findings.headline: Budget deficits of £845k in 2027/28 and £1.738m in 2028/29 with no agreed funding solution
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget balances, but the Medium Term Financial Strategy forecasts significant deficits in future years. These remain unfunded despite the council identifying savings and proposing further reductions. The council acknowledges the need for further options to bridge the gap but has not yet identified them.
findings.matters: Deficits of this size force the council to either make substantial service cuts, raise council tax sharply beyond inflation, or draw reserves. All three signal financial stress and constrain the council's flexibility.
findings.quote: Despite the increases in funding and budget savings identified in this report, there remain large forecast budget deficits of £0.845m in 2027/28 and £1.738m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H1: Treasury Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy of £41.8m dependent on continued low investment return environment
findings.detail: The council maintains an under-borrowed position by using reserves instead of external borrowing, explicitly justified by current low investment returns. This approach is conditional on economic conditions and accelerates reserve depletion.
findings.matters: If investment returns rise or economic conditions shift, this strategy becomes less attractive, risking either forced external borrowing at unfavourable rates or inadequate liquidity to meet obligations.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing position 2026/27 £41,750k; CFR £116,363k vs gross debt £74,613k
findings.quote: This strategy is prudent as investment returns are low and will be continued where possible.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H1: Treasury Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to revenue rising across planning period as capital programme generates ongoing debt service
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that the ratio of borrowing and financing costs to net revenue income is increasing over the three-year period, reflecting a £76.6m capital programme and the revenue claim this generates.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost ratios indicate a growing claim on revenue budget for debt service, constraining resources for service delivery and signalling longer-term sustainability questions.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure £76,619k (2025/26–2028/29); prudential borrowing requirement £9,931k; financing ratio increasing
findings.quote: The increasing ratio for the remainder of the budget period reflects the level of borrowing potentially required to finance the Council's planned Capital Programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H1: Treasury Strategy 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Working capital balances declining from £31.4m to £20.9m as internal borrowing strategy depletes reserves
findings.detail: The council's core funds and working balances are projected to reduce by £10.5m (33%) between 2025/26 and 2028/29. This material reduction is driven by the council's deliberate strategy of using its own cash reserves to finance capital expenditure internally rather than borrowing externally.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity buffers reduce the council's financial flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures and increase its dependence on external borrowing if reserves deplete further.
findings.quote: The projected reduction in investments is driven by the use of reserves / internal borrowing in financing the capital programme (see Table 2).

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Capital and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Major town centre regeneration project with £24.483m funding shortfall beyond government levelling up grant.
findings.detail: The council has secured £20m in government levelling up funding for a £44.483m town centre regeneration scheme, leaving a £24.483m gap that must be funded from council resources or other sources. This is a significant additional capital commitment at a time of budget pressure.
findings.matters: This project represents a large ongoing financial commitment that competes with core service funding and efficiency savings. If project costs overrun or economic conditions worsen, the council may struggle to fund both this project and maintain service quality.
findings.figures: £44.483m total project cost; £20m government funding; £24.483m funding gap
findings.quote: The council has successfully secured £20m from the government's levelling up fund for the regeneration of Chorley town centre, the total cost of the project is scheduled to cost £44.483m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Capital and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Council must deliver £0.845m revenue efficiency savings by 2027/28 through budget cuts and additional income generation.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy includes a mandatory efficiency savings target of £0.845m by 2027/28. These savings are to come from reduced revenue budgets and additional income generation, indicating the council faces revenue pressure.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver savings targets typically signals financial distress or service cuts. The council will face difficult choices if these targets cannot be met, particularly given the simultaneous budget gap forecast.
findings.figures: £0.845m revenue budget efficiency savings
findings.quote: The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a further £0.845m revenue budget efficiency savings to be realised by 2027/28. These savings will come through reduced revenue budgets and additional income generation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Capital and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement has risen from £49m to £116m primarily through large income-generating asset purchases, doubling debt burden.
findings.detail: The CFR has more than doubled since 2017/18, with most of the increase driven by the £33m Logistics House purchase and other capital projects intended to generate revenue. The council has deliberately borrowed significantly to fund income-generating assets.
findings.matters: This represents a major structural shift in the council's balance sheet. The debt is sustainable only if the anticipated investment income continues; if assets underperform or property values fall, the council would face debt-servicing difficulties.
findings.figures: CFR risen from approximately £49m (2017/18) to over £116m; £33m Logistics House purchase; net debt in 2026/27 must not exceed £116.363m
findings.quote: The council's capital financing requirement in 2017/18 was approximately £49m. The requirement then gradually rises as there has been significant developments undertaken within the borough such as Market Walk Extension, Primrose Gardens, Strawberry Fields, Strawberry Meadows and Tatton Gardens. The CFR has risen to over £116m, mainly due to the £33m purchase of the Logistics House site as well as borrowing to fund other large capital projects

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Capital and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Operating budgets are heavily dependent on income from capital investments, creating vulnerability if returns underperform.
findings.detail: Approximately 17.64% of the council's gross directorate budgets are funded by income generated from capital assets (Market Walk, Primrose Gardens, Strawberry Fields, Logistics House, and others). This income is essential to the operating budget and any shortfall would require significant service reductions or alternative funding.
findings.matters: A downturn in property values, rental income, or investment returns could impact one-sixth of the council's operating budgets, making it vulnerable to economic cycles.
findings.figures: 17.64% of gross directorate budgets; borrowing costs forecast at £4.099m by 2028/29; investment income forecast at £6.337m in 2028/29
findings.quote: The council's gross directorate budgets are funded by approximately 17.64% through the income generated by these assets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Capital and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Council forecasts a budget gap in coming years and is establishing flexible capital receipts tools to manage it.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it faces a forecast budget gap in the coming years and is introducing flexible use of capital receipts as a contingency tool. It notes that while it has no current plans to use these flexibilities, the measure addresses anticipated financial pressure.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council can close a forecast deficit through efficiency alone or will need to redirect capital receipts from infrastructure to revenue, limiting the council's capital investment capacity.
findings.figures: £0.845m efficiency savings to be realised by 2027/28
findings.quote: Given the forecast budget gap in the coming years and the prospect of Local Government Reorganisation the Council needs all the tools available to them that may be required in this period.

findings.paper_title: Chorley Borough Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL 19 Jan 26
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting implementation added £0.790m lease liabilities and £0.772m right-of-use assets to the balance sheet
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 (effective 1 April 2024) resulted in recognition of former operating leases on the balance sheet. The Council recognized £0.790m of lease liabilities and £0.772m of right-of-use assets. Auditors found no significant issues other than a disclosure amendment.
findings.matters: While implementation appears to have gone smoothly, IFRS 16 changes the treatment of lease obligations, affecting balance sheet structure and comparability. A £0.790m liability now appears on-balance that was previously off-balance.
findings.figures: Lease liabilities £0.790m; right of use assets £0.772m
findings.quote: The implementation of IFRS 16 has resulted in £0.790m of lease liabilities and £0.772m Right of Use Assets recognised on the balance sheet in respect of former operating leases.

findings.paper_title: Chorley Borough Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL 19 Jan 26
findings.headline: Pension fund position moved to a liability of £2.356m, a significant estimate sensitive to actuarial assumptions
findings.detail: The Council's pension fund position shifted from a prior-year net asset to a net defined benefit liability of £2.356m. This represents a significant accounting estimate due to size and sensitivity to changes in key assumptions (discount rate, inflation rate, salary increase, life expectancy). Auditors confirmed completeness and accuracy of member data provided to the actuary and challenged actuarial assumptions using PWC as auditor's expert.
findings.matters: A shift to pension liability of £2.356m affects the Council's net worth and future funding requirements. Material movements in pension valuations signal changing obligations that impact long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Pension fund net liability £2.356m (2024-25)
findings.quote: The 2024-25 pension fund net liability of £2.356m is considered a significant estimate due to the size of the numbers involved and the sensitivity of the estimate to changes in key assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Chorley Borough Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL 19 Jan 26
findings.headline: Significant IT control deficiencies including no cyber supplier risk assessments, no vulnerability management process, and no privileged user activity reviews
findings.detail: Auditors identified multiple IT control gaps: Council is working toward MHCLG cyber assessment framework compliance (target March 2026) but cyber incident response plans remain in draft; no process exists for identifying or mitigating cybersecurity risks from external suppliers; no formal vulnerability management process despite patches being performed; no user access reviews in the last 12 months; no monitoring of privileged user activities; no logging or monitoring of scheduled IT system changes.
findings.matters: These governance gaps expose the Council to reputational and operational risk from cyber incidents, and fail to meet GDPR safeguard requirements. For a lender, they represent organizational control weaknesses that could impact service continuity and financial stability.
findings.figures: 43% of UK organisations reported experiencing a cyber breach or attack in the last 12 months (per Department for Science, Innovation and Technology April 2025)
findings.quote: we note that the Council is working to achieve a cyber security policy that is fully compliant with MHCLG's cyber assessment framework (CAF). The Council has submitted its plan to MHCLG however, it still has a number of actions to complete, which it aims to achieve by March 2026... there is currently no process of identifying and mitigating cybersecurity risks posed by its external suppliers... the Council has no formal vulnerability management process in place... no user access reviews have taken place over the last 12 months and there has been no regular review of activities performed by privileged users.

findings.paper_title: Chorley Borough Council Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL 19 Jan 26
findings.headline: Property valuation errors required £3.720m in corrections, with new valuer engaged without signed terms of engagement
findings.detail: Auditors identified multiple valuation errors totaling £1.160m overstatement across land, buildings and car parks (due to incorrect BCIS location factors, wrong valuation figures, and misapplied car park income), plus a separate £2.560m downward revaluation of Astley Hall (from £10.59m to £8.028m). The Council engaged a new valuer (Align Property Partners) for 2024-25 but did not have a signed terms of engagement in place before work commenced.
findings.matters: Large corrected errors in asset valuations (£3.720m total) demonstrate control weaknesses in the valuation process. The absence of signed terms of engagement with a new valuer represents a governance gap that could recur.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £135.524m; investment properties £35.458m; corrections: £0.221m understatement, £0.930m overstatement, £0.050m overstatement, £0.059m understatement, £0.460m overstatement (net £1.160m), plus Astley Hall £2.560m downward revaluation
findings.quote: Incorrect BCIS (build cost information service rates) location factor had been used in determining the valuation of four assets. The impact on the Council's land and buildings was an understatement of £0.221m... The overall impact of the above is an overstatement in the valuation of the Council's property, plant and equipment of £1.160m. Management have chosen to amend for this. Our review of the valuation for Astley Hall (£10.59m) concluded that the BCIS rates used were not deemed to be the most appropriate for a historic building like Astley Hall. As a result a revised valuation was obtained which resulted in a new valuation of £8.028m, a decrease of £2.560m.

news_drafts.lead: A rising financing cost ratio reduces the council's flexibility to respond to other pressures and increases the structural cost of its existing debt. For a lender, this indicates less headroom for managing revenue volatility.

news_drafts.lead: Working balances are the buffer against unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. A £12.9m variance on a revised estimate signals the council could not maintain expected liquidity, which matters to lenders assessing financial resilience.

news_drafts.headline: Major local government reorganisation scheduled for 2028 — councils transitioning from two-tier to new structure
news_drafts.lead: Major structural reorganisation creates uncertainty and diverts senior management capacity away from current operations. It presents a material governance risk period with potential for control gaps as responsibilities shift between organisations.
